Design Your Product

Pick a garment, fabric, colour and decoration technique, upload your logo and see how it would look. Send it to us and your exact configuration arrives with the enquiry.

PNG or SVG with a transparent background previews best. Up to 10 MB. Your file is attached to the enquiry and is never published.

Drag the logo on the preview to move it, or use Logo size to scale it.

This is a preview, not a photograph of your order. The garment is a stock product photograph of a blank; your logo is drawn on to show placement, scale and the character of each decoration technique so we can agree the brief. Thread and print colours are matched to Pantone at sampling, not on screen.

Embroidery

Your logo is stitched into the garment with thread on a computerised embroidery machine. The design is first converted into a stitch file (called digitising).

Best for
Logos, crests and small text on hoodies, sweatshirts and jackets. It looks premium and lasts as long as the garment.
Limits
Very fine detail and tiny text (roughly under 5 mm tall) can blur. Gradients and photographs cannot be stitched. Large areas get heavy and stiff.

3D puff embroidery

Embroidery stitched over a foam layer, so the design stands up from the fabric with a raised, rounded edge.

Best for
Bold logos, initials and simple shapes on the front of hoodies, sweatshirts and jackets.
Limits
Needs bold, simple shapes with thick strokes. Thin lines and small text do not puff well. Not suited to large back designs.

Sublimation

Ink is turned into a gas with heat and bonds into polyester fibres, so the print becomes part of the fabric and can run edge to edge.

Best for
All-over patterns, full-colour designs and teamwear where the whole garment is the design.
Limits
Only works on light-coloured, polyester-rich fabric. It does not work on cotton fleece or dark garments.

DTF (direct-to-film) print

Your design is printed onto a film with a white base layer, then heat-pressed onto the garment.

Best for
Full-colour logos on most fabrics and colours, including dark cotton fleece, at small and medium quantities.
Limits
Leaves a thin, slightly smooth layer on the fabric. Large solid areas feel less breathable than screen print.

DTG (direct-to-garment) print

An inkjet printer prints the design straight into the fabric, a bit like a paper printer.

Best for
Detailed, full-colour artwork and photographic designs on cotton-rich garments.
Limits
Best on high-cotton fabric. Colours can look softer on dark garments, and it is slower for large runs.

Screen printing

Ink is pushed through a fine mesh screen, one screen per colour, onto the garment.

Best for
Larger runs of the same design with a few solid colours. Durable and good value at volume.
Limits
Each colour needs its own screen, so set-up makes small runs and many-colour designs less economical. Photographic gradients are limited.

High-density print

A thick screen-printing ink built up in layers to create a raised, sharp-edged print you can feel.

Best for
Bold logos and lettering where you want texture without stitching.
Limits
Works best with simple shapes and few colours. Fine detail is lost as the ink builds up.

HD / heat-transfer vinyl

Coloured vinyl is cut to the shape of your design and heat-pressed onto the garment. HD vinyl is a thicker version with a raised finish.

Best for
Names, numbers and simple one or two-colour logos, especially for teamwear and leavers hoodies.
Limits
Best for solid shapes and text. Very detailed or multi-colour artwork is not practical, and it can crack with heavy wear.

Rhinestone

Small glass or resin stones are laid out in the shape of your design and heat-fixed onto the garment.

Best for
Eye-catching logos, dance and cheer teams, and leavers designs that need sparkle.
Limits
Designs are made of dots, so fine lines and small text are simplified. Needs gentle washing inside out.
